description: We are pepe & javi, the team behind Planet Pulse. We share an interest in space, technology and creative ways to communicate science. Carlos focuses on the concept and digital experience, while Ramon explores rhythm, sound and storytelling. Together, we want to make Earth's moving systems easier to explore through an accessible listening experience. We welcome ideas from people interested in Earth science, sonification and inclusive design.
summary:
Planet Pulse is a concept for an accessible Earth Jukebox that turns ocean motion into an understandable sound experience. It would pair NASA Earth Information Center visualizations with audio generated during playback: current speed would control pulse rate, temperature would control pitch, and spoken cues would explain direction and missing data.

Users would select a region, explore a timeline and compare two moments using consistent sound scales. Keyboard controls, text alternatives and adjustable audio layers would support different access needs.

We developed a project concept and a seven-slide presentation using NASA's Global Sea Surface Currents and Temperature visualization as a reference. No working application or audio engine has been implemented, and no numerical datasets have been processed. The intended impact is to help students, museum visitors and people with visual impairments explore how our planet moves through complementary visual, auditory and textual experiences.
details:
PROJECT CONCEPT

Planet Pulse proposes an interactive listening experience for ocean circulation. It addresses The Earth Information Jukebox challenge by pairing visual frames with meaningful sound generated during playback.

USER EXPERIENCE

Users would choose an ocean region and an available historical time period, listen to reference sounds and explore a synchronized timeline. They could pause, replay or compare two dates using consistent mapping scales. Each track would display its source, units and time coverage.

HOW IT WOULD WORK

Current speed would control pulse frequency: faster flow would produce a faster pulse. Sea surface temperature would control pitch: warmer values would produce higher tones. Spoken bearings would explain direction, while a distinct cue would identify missing values.

Users could isolate individual sound layers. Reference examples and fixed scales would help them understand what they hear.

NASA RESOURCES

The reference case is NASA Scientific Visualization Studio's Global Sea Surface Currents and Temperature visualization, based on ECCO2 model output and included in the Earth Information Center gallery.

A numerical implementation would require compatible data with matching timestamps, units and spatial coverage. Visual particle motion would not be treated as a direct measurement of current speed.

ACCESSIBILITY AND IMPACT

The concept includes keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels, text descriptions, adjustable volume and separate audio controls. Users could explore through sound, visuals or text according to their needs.

Potential settings include classrooms, museums and independent learning. The intended benefits would require evaluation with users, including blind and low-vision listeners.

PROPOSED TECHNOLOGY

A possible implementation would use HTML, CSS and JavaScript, a preprocessing step to align data with visualization frames, and browser audio synthesis. Audio would be generated during playback of historical content, rather than presented as a live data feed.

CURRENT STATUS

The deliverables are a seven-slide presentation and a written proposal. No application, audio engine or data pipeline has been implemented. No numerical datasets have been processed and no user testing has taken place.
